newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia meat bodies may be split - review.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia meat bodies may be split - review.

text.p: A major government review of Australia's red meat industry has presented as a preferred option the splitting of the main industry statutory body the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp into two separate entities.

The majority recommendation of the Meat and Livestock Industry Reform task force is that two product-focused corporations -- for beef and sheepmeat -- be established to replace the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC), a report issued by the Australian government said.
The bodies would be non-profit and non-statutory, with each body to be funded by compulsory producer levies, it said.

The report recommends that the industry's three existing statutory authorities, the Meat Research Corp (MRC), the AMLC and the Meat Industry Council (MIC), should be abolished as statutory structures and replaced with two non-statutory boards.
The two non-statutory authorities would draw on separate industry contributor trust accounts, it said.

Separate producer trust accounts would be established by the corporations for marketing and research, monitored by the federal government and industry shareholders through annual reports and annual general meetings.
Board members would predominantly come from the industry.
A minority recommendation calls for a single meat corporation with one board and separate operational units in beef marketing, sheepmeat marketing, research and development and quality systems.
Another minority recommendation calls for a single meat corporation with one board and separate operational units in beef marketing, sheepmeat marketing, research and development and quality systems.
Another option, also a minority recommendation, calls for a single meat corporation with two product-focused business units, each with marketing, research and development and quality systems.
Separate and independent annual reviews of corporate performance are called for in the report.
"This is a report on reform for the future," Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said. It would provide a firm basis for discussion, he said.
